title: Ramadan: seclusion
hookLine: in the last ten nights many stay in the mosque in prayer

cards: Late at night in the last ten days of Ramadan, a corner of a large mosque can look like a campsite. Sleeping bags. A small curtain strung between pillars.
A Qur'an, a water bottle, a phone switched off and tucked away. Someone has moved in. Not for a night, but for ten days, leaving only for what they truly must.
They're not there because they have nowhere else to go. They have homes, jobs, families. They've stepped out of all of it, on purpose.

teach.h: I'TIKAF: TO STAY, TO KEEP TO IT.
teach.b: This is i'tikaf. The word means staying at something, keeping yourself to it. A person stays in the mosque with the intention of devoting themselves to God: prayer, Qur'an, remembrance, quiet.

teach.h: THE LAST TEN DAYS, EVERY YEAR.
teach.b: The Qur'an mentions it in Surah Al-Baqarah, in the verses about fasting, as people staying in the mosques. 'A'isha reports, in Bukhari, that the Prophet ﷺ used to spend the last ten days of every Ramadan in i'tikaf until he died, and that his wives kept the practice after him.

teach.h: WAITING FOR THE NIGHT OF POWER.
teach.b: Because somewhere in them is Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. A hadith tells Muslims to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten. So i'tikaf is a way of being present for whichever night it turns out to be.
Schools of law differ on details: how long it must last, and whether a woman may keep it in a prayer space at home, as the Hanafis allow, or in the mosque, as others teach.
Some who can't take ten days keep a single day, or a night. And here's a human detail Bukhari keeps. While the Prophet was in i'tikaf, his wife Safiyya came to visit him one night.
They talked, and when she rose to go home, he got up and walked her back. Withdrawal in this picture isn't coldness. It's closing the door on the noise, not on the people you love.
Withdraw to draw near: the outer world gets smaller, so that something else can get larger.

how: In the last ten days of Ramadan, some Muslims stay in the mosque in i'tikaf, leaving only for essential needs; others keep it for a day or a night, and practice for women varies between schools of law.

o: a fast kept on the Night of Power alone
the night prayer recited in long sections
staying in the mosque in devotion, a retreat

p: to stay at, to keep to it

s: i'tikaf is for people with nowhere else to go
it's a chosen retreat: people with homes and families step away on purpose.
the Prophet kept i'tikaf in the last ten days of Ramadan until he died
'A'isha reports it in Bukhari, and his wives kept it after him.
in i'tikaf, the Prophet refused to see his family
Safiyya visited him, and he walked her home.

games.q: the Prophet is in i'tikaf in the mosque. his wife Safiyya visits one evening, and when she gets up to leave it's dark. what does he do?
o: get up and walk her back home.
ask someone else to take her.
games.why: he got up and walked Safiyya back. Bukhari keeps the detail: withdrawal isn't coldness.

practice: Close a door if you can, and put your phone in another room, or face down and silent: for these few minutes, the world is a little smaller on purpose.
If you pray, give the time to prayer or a few verses of the Qur'an; if you don't, give it to quiet.

wordCard.voice: I'tikaf. Staying in the mosque in devotion, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan: withdrawing from the world to draw near. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: i'tikaf, devotional retreat in the mosque.

carryVoice: Your line: withdraw to draw near. Ten days, a night, or a few quiet minutes. See you tomorrow.
